Answering it well requires understanding both the mechanisms (quorum configuration, synchronous vs. asynchronous replication) and the actual business cost of staleness for each specific feature, not assuming stronger is always better or that weaker is always an acceptable shortcut.

assessments.prompt: A cluster has N=5 replicas, configured with W=3 and R=3. Per the pigeonhole-principle argument in the concept, why does this configuration guarantee a read will see the most recent write?
options: Because 3 out of 5 replicas is a majority, and majorities are defined to always be up to date.

Because W + R (3 + 3 = 6) exceeds N (5), so the set of replicas acknowledging the write and the set of replicas queried by the read cannot be fully disjoint -- at least one replica must belong to both sets and will have recorded the write.
Because the write is always sent to the same 3 replicas that the read later queries, by convention.
Because with W=3 and R=3, all 5 replicas are updated synchronously before the write is acknowledged.
assessments.explanation: The concept's quorum example lays this out explicitly as a pigeonhole-principle argument: two sets of size 3 drawn from a pool of 5 cannot be fully disjoint, since 3+3=6 exceeds 5, so at least one replica must be common to both the write's acknowledging set and the read's querying set. Option A invents an unrelated, incorrect definition of "majority." Option C is false -- the concept never claims the specific replicas are the same each time, only that overlap is mathematically guaranteed regardless of which specific replicas happen to be chosen. Option D is wrong -- with W=3, only 3 of the 5 replicas need to acknowledge the write, not all 5.

assessments.prompt: Per the concept's comparison of synchronous and asynchronous replication, what is the specific risk of asynchronous replication that is easy to forget when only thinking about read staleness?
options: Asynchronous replication makes every write permanently unrecoverable, even before any failure occurs.
If the leader fails before a write has replicated to a follower, and that follower is then promoted to leader, an already-acknowledged write can be lost entirely -- not just delayed.
Asynchronous replication requires twice the network bandwidth of synchronous replication under all conditions.
Asynchronous replication prevents the system from ever using quorum reads or writes.
assessments.explanation: The concept calls this out explicitly as a closing risk: with asynchronous replication, "if the leader fails before replicating, a write acknowledged to the client can be LOST if a follower is promoted without it" -- a data-loss risk distinct from, and easy to overlook alongside, the more commonly discussed replication-lag/staleness issue. Option A overstates the risk into an absolute that isn't what's described -- most writes do replicate successfully; the risk is specifically about the failure-before-replication window. Option C is a fabricated bandwidth claim not discussed anywhere in the concept. Option D is false -- quorum mechanics are a separate, compatible concept from sync/async replication mode.

assessments.prompt: Per the concept's "match, don't maximize" framing, why is applying strong consistency to every operation in a system, including a rarely-changing product description page, considered a mistake even if the system "can afford" the performance cost?
options: Because strong consistency is technically impossible to implement for read-only pages.

Because it pays real coordination latency and reduced availability-under-partition on every operation, including the vast majority where nobody would ever have noticed staleness anyway -- the goal is matching each operation's actual requirement, not maximizing the guarantee wherever budget allows.
Because strong consistency can only be applied to numeric fields, not text content like product descriptions.
Because product description pages are always sharded, and sharded data cannot use strong consistency.
assessments.explanation: The concept's misconception states this directly: strong consistency "reduces availability under partition... and adds coordination latency to every single operation using it, including the vast majority of operations where nobody would ever have noticed staleness anyway -- the actual engineering skill is matching the guarantee to each operation's real requirement, not maximizing consistency wherever the budget allows." Option A is false -- strong consistency is technically implementable for read-only pages; the concept's objection is about cost-effectiveness, not feasibility. Options C and D are fabricated technical constraints that appear nowhere in the material.
